title: The Dungeons of Doria Prototype - Part 2 - Game Discussion
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y_mkJt3oY_k

Having toured the components, Daniel (@dungeondive) plays Dungeons of Doria and reports back on what works. The character system draws the strongest praise: like a FromSoftware game, your starting class only sets your opening stats and gear. Levelling puts points into raw attributes, and since every item has attribute requirements, you build your character toward the loot you find rather than down a class track. He demonstrates by drawing six random cards and speccing a character around a shield-blade.

The initiative and action-point system gets a full worked example. Roll 2d10 plus initiative for your pool, and whoever sits highest acts — spending points on movement, revealing rooms, searching, attacking — so turns interleave rather than run one player at a time. The tactical wrinkle he loves: your final action of a round may push you into negative points, so a 15-point hammer is best swung last.

Armour breaks when used to negate damage and must be repaired, with whole sets repairable for the cost of the priciest piece. Double ones fumble, and on an initiative roll that costs you the entire round.

The criticisms are specific: the initiative track is visually cluttered despite being the game's core, starting weapons can't hurt armoured level-one monsters unless you take the warrior, and the rules say "adjacent" where they mean orthogonal.

----

Is "build toward the loot you find" a better RPG hook than picking a class up front?
